angler._note: The angler: a cartoony fisher with a bushy ginger beard, a big round nose, a bucket hat, a tan fishing vest over a shirt in the player's colour, khaki trousers and green rubber boots, holding a rod in the right mitten. No boxes: the limbs are tapered eight-sided tubes (wide at the shoulder and thigh, narrow at the wrist and ankle), the head a twelve-sided ball, the beard a wedge, the hat a short cone with a flared brim, the vest a twelve-sided tapered body with a slight belly. Elbows and knees bend without a gap: the faces between the upper and lower part of each limb join vertices of both parts. The origin is between the feet; the angler faces +z and stands 1.62 m to the top of the hat. drive: seated on the back bench, right hand back on the tiller, left hand on the knee, rod put away (scale 0). fish: standing, the right hand on the reel and the left on the butt, rod held out over the bow. idle: a slow sway. Anchors: line is the rod's tip, where the fishing line starts; wrist_l is on the left forearm's middle, on its axis, where the Fish-Boy straps on (the forearm runs down -y at rest, the back of the wrist faces +x, its radius is about 45 mm).
angler.name: Angler

birch._note: A slender birch: a white five-sided trunk with dark bark marks, leaning a little, under three faceted clumps of leaves, about 6.7 m tall. Prop conventions: the pivot is the middle of the base at the origin; y 0 is the ground (the water's surface for things standing in water). Flat colours from one lake palette, muted so the water and the players' boats stand out in fog.
birch.name: Birch

black-crappie._note: Black crappie (Pomoxis nigromaculatus), an uncommon schooling panfish of Midwest lakes. Markings from field-guide descriptions: a deep, very flat, silvery body speckled all over with black, a dark olive back, a dip over the eye to an upturned mouth, a big eye, and a big dorsal fin (seven or eight spines) mirrored by an anal fin almost as big, both set far back and speckled like the body.
black-crappie.name: Black crappie

bluegill._note: Bluegill (Lepomis macrochirus), a common sunfish of Midwest lakes. Markings from field-guide descriptions: a deep, round, flat body; olive back; 6 to 8 dark vertical bars on the sides; an orange-yellow breast; a solid black ear flap at the back of the gill cover; a dark spot at the rear of the soft dorsal fin; a small mouth. From above, as seen from a boat: thin, as a sunfish is (about a sixth as wide as it is long), widest just behind the gills, with long pointed pectoral fins swept back along the body. The dorsal and anal fins are thin wedges and the tail a thin blade, as on a real fish, so the fins read from the side and the tail fans out as it swims (SECOND-ORDER R2.130-R2.139). 170 mm long, the base length (SECOND-ORDER R1.150-R1.169).
bluegill.name: Bluegill

boat._note: The player's boat: a chunky aluminium fishing boat about 13 ft long, painted in the player's colour, with a back bench by the outboard, a middle bench and a raised casting deck at the bow. The origin is on the waterline under the middle of the boat; the bow points +z. Anchors: drive is the floor where the seated driver's feet rest (hips on the back bench, right hand on the tiller); fish is the casting deck where the angler stands.
boat.name: Boat

bobber._note: The bobber on every player's line: a round two-tone float about 50 mm across, red below and white above with a dark seam, a short white stem and button on top, and the eyelet for the line underneath. It rides on the water and dips when a fish nibbles (the game moves it). Drawn larger than life from the boat camera (look.json fishing.bobber_scale_pct). The origin is its middle, on the waterline.
bobber.name: Bobber

boulder._note: A big rounded glacial boulder, about 2.2 m across and 1.4 m tall, sunk a little into the ground. Prop conventions: the pivot is the middle of the base at the origin; y 0 is the ground (the water's surface for things standing in water). Flat colours from one lake palette, muted so the water and the players' boats stand out in fog.
boulder.name: Boulder

cabin._note: A small log cabin with a pitched roof, a stone chimney, a door on the +z side and a window on each long side: 4 m by 3.2 m, about 4.3 m to the chimney top. Prop conventions: the pivot is the middle of the base at the origin; y 0 is the ground (the water's surface for things standing in water). Flat colours from one lake palette, muted so the water and the players' boats stand out in fog.
cabin.name: Cabin

cattails._note: A clump of cattails and reed blades standing in shallow water: three stalks with brown heads and six blades, about 1.8 m above the water. Prop conventions: the pivot is the middle of the base at the origin; y 0 is the ground (the water's surface for things standing in water). Flat colours from one lake palette, muted so the water and the players' boats stand out in fog.
cattails.name: Cattails

channel-catfish._note: Channel catfish (Ictalurus punctatus), a rare whiskered bottom feeder of Midwest lakes and rivers. Shape (v4, checked against the real fish from the side, above and 3/4): a broad, flat head about a quarter of the length, wider than it is deep, with a blunt snout rounded from above and the wide mouth a little under it (the upper jaw longer); small eyes high on the head; a thick, round body, deepest ahead of the middle, flattening toward the head and pressed thin toward the tail; a short dorsal fin set forward with a stout spine; a small fleshy adipose fin; a long, round-edged anal fin; pelvic fins under the middle; spined pectorals low behind the head; a deeply forked tail with two about equal, rounded lobes. Markings from field-guide descriptions: no scales; eight barbels ("whiskers"), the two at the corners of the mouth longest; slate grey-blue above, paler blue-grey sides with scattered small dark spots, a white belly.
channel-catfish.name: Channel catfish

dock._note: A small wooden dock on six posts: the shore end is at the origin and the deck runs 4.8 m out along +z, 0.5 m above the water (y 0). The posts reach 1 m below it to the bed. Prop conventions: the pivot is the middle of the base at the origin; y 0 is the ground (the water's surface for things standing in water). Flat colours from one lake palette, muted so the water and the players' boats stand out in fog.
dock.name: Dock

eelgrass._note: Eelgrass: a tuft of nine long ribbon blades, 0.9 to 1.2 m, leaning out and swaying in the current, on sandy shallow beds. Prop conventions: the pivot is the middle of the base at the origin; y 0 is the lake bed. Flat colours from one lake palette.
eelgrass.name: Eelgrass

fallen-log._note: A fallen trunk lying along z, 3.8 m long, with pale cut ends, moss on top and one broken branch. Prop conventions: the pivot is the middle of the base at the origin; y 0 is the ground (the water's surface for things standing in water). Flat colours from one lake palette, muted so the water and the players' boats stand out in fog.
fallen-log.name: Fallen log

fishboy._note: The Fish-Boy: the angler's wrist computer, strapped to the left forearm (the hand toward +x). Its screen is the part "screen": one flat 192 x 108 mm rectangle (16:9) at z = 0 facing +z, with the anchor "screen" at its middle; the game draws the radar, the Fishpedia and the minigames on it. The bezel is 12 mm at the sides and 7 mm above and below, its front 3 mm proud of the screen, so a view that fits the screen to 80% of its width and height shows the bezel in the next 10% and the world in the last 10% (at a 50 degree field of view: 80%, 92%). The case hides behind the bezel there; the dial, the antenna, the knobs and the arm show at the edges. A tackle-box case: green with a cream stripe, brass rivets, a bobber dial, two knobs, three tab keys, a rod-tip antenna, a reel crank and a brass fish on the hand side. The sleeve takes the player's colour.
fishboy.name: Fish-Boy

item-buoy._note: The item buoy: a giant red and white fishing bobber floating upright, about 1.5 m across and 2.6 m above the water. Its middle seam glows as if something lit sits inside, and a glowing beacon with a halo and four twinkling sparkles tops its striped antenna, so it reads as "something inside" through fog. A spoon lure dangles on a line below. It bobs on the swell, and once a loop it dips and pops back up as if something nibbled. The origin is on the waterline at its middle.
item-buoy.name: Item buoy

lake-sturgeon._note: Lake sturgeon (Acipenser fulvescens), a legendary giant of the Great Lakes and big Midwest lakes, older than the dinosaurs in shape. Markings from field-guide descriptions: long and shark-like, grey-brown to olive with a pale belly, a pointed cone of a snout with four barbels under it and the mouth beneath, five rows of bony plates (scutes) along the back and sides, and a shark-like tail whose upper lobe is much longer than the lower. From above, as seen from a boat: a conical, rounded shovel of a snout narrower than the head, wide-spread pectoral fins, the body widest just behind them and tapering long to the shark-like tail. The dorsal and anal fins are thin wedges and the tail a thin blade, as on a real fish, so the fins read from the side and the tail fans out as it swims (SECOND-ORDER R2.130-R2.139). 1500 mm long, the base length (SECOND-ORDER R1.150-R1.169).
lake-sturgeon.name: Lake sturgeon

lake-trout._note: Lake trout (Salvelinus namaycush), a rare fish of cold, deep northern Michigan lakes such as Burt Lake. Markings from field-guide descriptions: a long, streamlined char; dark grey-green covered in pale cream spots (light spots on a dark ground, head and fins included), a pale belly, a big mouth reaching past the eye, a small adipose fin, white leading edges on the lower fins, and a deeply forked tail.
lake-trout.name: Lake trout

largemouth-bass._note: Largemouth bass (Micropterus salmoides), an uncommon prize of weedy Midwest lakes, the biggest of the black basses. Markings from field-guide descriptions: green back, pale green sides and a white belly, one broad, ragged dark stripe along the middle of each side, a huge mouth whose upper jaw reaches past the back of the eye, and a dorsal fin notched almost into two. A smallmouth is bronze with vertical bars and its jaw stops below the eye.
largemouth-bass.name: Largemouth bass

lily-pads._note: A floating cluster of five notched lily pads and one flower, about 1.7 m across, on the water's surface (y 0). They bob on the swell. Prop conventions: the pivot is the middle of the base at the origin; y 0 is the ground (the water's surface for things standing in water). Flat colours from one lake palette, muted so the water and the players' boats stand out in fog.
lily-pads.name: Lily pads

lily-stems._note: The stems of a lily pad clump: four thin stems curving up from one root on the bed to the pads above. One metre tall: the scene stretches it to the water's depth. Prop conventions: the pivot is the middle of the base at the origin; y 0 is the lake bed. Flat colours from one lake palette.
lily-stems.name: Lily stems

lure._note: The lure under each bobber: a spoon about 60 mm long, a convex teardrop with a silver face and an orange back, hanging nose up from its split ring, with a single hook and a red tag below. It flutters and turns slowly in the water. The origin is the split ring, where the line ties on.
lure.name: Lure

muskellunge._note: Muskellunge (Esox masquinongy), the legendary "fish of ten thousand casts" of Midwest lakes. Markings from field-guide descriptions: shaped like a pike but bigger, light silvery-olive to bronze with DARK bars or spots on a light ground (a pike is the reverse), fins and dorsal set far back, and sharply pointed tail lobes. From above, as seen from a boat: a long, even body with a long head tapering to a flat duck-bill snout with nearly parallel sides and a rounded tip, the dorsal and anal fins near the tail. The dorsal and anal fins are thin wedges and the tail a thin blade, as on a real fish, so the fins read from the side and the tail fans out as it swims (SECOND-ORDER R2.130-R2.139). 950 mm long, the base length (SECOND-ORDER R1.150-R1.169).
muskellunge.name: Muskellunge

northern-pike._note: Northern pike (Esox lucius), a rare ambush hunter of weedy Midwest lakes. Markings from field-guide descriptions: long and torpedo-shaped with a flat duck-bill snout, dark green with rows of LIGHT bean-shaped spots, a cream belly, the dorsal and anal fins far back by the tail, and reddish fins with dark marks. From above, as seen from a boat: a long, even body with a long head tapering to a flat duck-bill snout with nearly parallel sides and a rounded tip, the dorsal and anal fins near the tail. The dorsal and anal fins are thin wedges and the tail a thin blade, as on a real fish, so the fins read from the side and the tail fans out as it swims (SECOND-ORDER R2.130-R2.139). 650 mm long, the base length (SECOND-ORDER R1.150-R1.169).
northern-pike.name: Northern pike

pine-small._note: A young pine: two fat star-edged tiers, about 3.6 m tall. Prop conventions: the pivot is the middle of the base at the origin; y 0 is the ground (the water's surface for things standing in water). Flat colours from one lake palette, muted so the water and the players' boats stand out in fog.
pine-small.name: Young pine

pine-tall._note: A tall narrow spruce: four star-edged tiers, about 9.2 m tall. Prop conventions: the pivot is the middle of the base at the origin; y 0 is the ground (the water's surface for things standing in water). Flat colours from one lake palette, muted so the water and the players' boats stand out in fog.
pine-tall.name: Tall spruce

pine._note: A chunky cartoon pine: three star-edged tiers on a short trunk, about 6.7 m tall. Prop conventions: the pivot is the middle of the base at the origin; y 0 is the ground (the water's surface for things standing in water). Flat colours from one lake palette, muted so the water and the players' boats stand out in fog.
pine.name: Pine

pondweed._note: Pondweed: four tapered stems up to 1.5 m with lance-shaped leaves on alternate sides, swaying in the current. Grows on the lake bed in shallow water near reed beds. Prop conventions: the pivot is the middle of the base at the origin; y 0 is the lake bed. Flat colours from one lake palette.
pondweed.name: Pondweed

pumpkinseed._note: Pumpkinseed (Lepomis gibbosus), a common sunfish of weedy Midwest shallows, smaller and rounder than the bluegill. Markings from field-guide descriptions: a deep, round, flat body; olive-gold sides covered in orange and yellow spots; an orange-yellow breast; wavy blue-green lines across the orange cheek; a black ear flap with a bright red-orange spot on its rear edge; long, pointed pectoral fins; a small mouth.
pumpkinseed.name: Pumpkinseed

reed-stems._note: The underwater stalks of a clump of cattails: three round stalks and six blade bases from the bed up to the surface, under the Cattails model's own stalks. One metre tall: the scene stretches it to the water's depth. Prop conventions: the pivot is the middle of the base at the origin; y 0 is the lake bed. Flat colours from one lake palette.
reed-stems.name: Reed stems

rock-bass._note: Rock bass (Ambloplites rupestris), a common sunfish of rocky Midwest shores, chunkier than a bluegill. Markings from field-guide descriptions: olive to brassy-brown with a dark spot on each scale, so the sides show rows of dark spots; a big bright red eye; a large mouth reaching below the eye; a white belly; a spiny dorsal fin joined to the soft one, and a big anal fin with six spines.
rock-bass.name: Rock bass

shore-rocks._note: A low flat slab with a smaller stone beside it, for the water's edge: about 3.6 m across and 0.7 m tall. Prop conventions: the pivot is the middle of the base at the origin; y 0 is the ground (the water's surface for things standing in water). Flat colours from one lake palette, muted so the water and the players' boats stand out in fog.
shore-rocks.name: Shore rocks

smallmouth-bass._note: Smallmouth bass (Micropterus dolomieu), an uncommon fighter of rocky Midwest lakes. Markings from field-guide descriptions: bronze to brown-olive, with faint dark vertical bars on the sides, dark bars radiating back from a red eye across the cheek, a joined dorsal fin with a shallow notch, and a jaw that ends below the eye. From above, as seen from a boat: a chunky torpedo about a fifth as wide as it is long, widest a third of the way back just behind the gill covers, the head tapering smoothly to a rounded point. The dorsal and anal fins are thin wedges and the tail a thin blade, as on a real fish, so the fins read from the side and the tail fans out as it swims (SECOND-ORDER R2.130-R2.139). 350 mm long, the base length (SECOND-ORDER R1.150-R1.169).
smallmouth-bass.name: Smallmouth bass

walleye._note: Walleye (Sander vitreus), an uncommon prize of Midwest lakes. Markings from field-guide descriptions: long and rounded, olive-gold with darker saddles over the back, a white belly, a large glassy eye, two separate dorsal fins with a dark spot at the rear base of the first, and a white tip on the lower lobe of the tail. From above, as seen from a boat: a slim, round-bodied torpedo about an eighth as wide as it is long, the head tapering to a pointed snout. The dorsal and anal fins are thin wedges and the tail a thin blade, as on a real fish, so the fins read from the side and the tail fans out as it swims (SECOND-ORDER R2.130-R2.139). 430 mm long, the base length (SECOND-ORDER R1.150-R1.169).
walleye.name: Walleye

yellow-perch._note: Yellow perch (Perca flavescens), a common schooling fish of Midwest lakes. Markings from field-guide descriptions: golden-yellow sides with six to eight dark vertical bars that run down from an olive back, a white belly, two separate dorsal fins (the first spiny, with a dark blotch at its rear), and orange lower fins. From above, as seen from a boat: a slim torpedo about a sixth as wide as it is long, widest under the first dorsal fin, the snout tapering to a point. The dorsal and anal fins are thin wedges and the tail a thin blade, as on a real fish, so the fins read from the side and the tail fans out as it swims (SECOND-ORDER R2.130-R2.139). 200 mm long, the base length (SECOND-ORDER R1.150-R1.169).
yellow-perch.name: Yellow perch
